content: 1. Strengthening primary healthcare (PHC) services, expanding diagnostic and testing capabilities, and implementing social protection schemes where necessary can help reduce both direct and indirect costs for children, adolescents, and their caregivers when seeking care. This approach also addresses the specific needs of vulnerable groups. 2. Flexible models of engagement tailored to local contexts are essential due to the diversity of health markets. Standardization in public-private mix (PPM) models may limit scalability and effectiveness. 3. Digital technologies should be leveraged to improve data collection and reporting. Traditional paper-based tools used by National Tuberculosis Programs (NTPs) may delay accurate reporting, especially from the private sector, including data on pediatric and adolescent tuberculosis (TB). Digital tools can enable the collection of more granular, age-disaggregated data and support data-driven decision-making. 4. Financial and non-financial incentives, when well-designed, can motivate healthcare providers to actively participate in TB prevention and care efforts. 5. Continuous monitoring and evaluation of public-private mix (PPM) contributions are critical to achieving sustainability and accountability. The NTP must ensure that aspects of pediatric and adolescent TB are included in the monitoring and evaluation framework. 6. The CaP-TB project in India, funded by Unitaid, aimed to improve the quality of TB care in the private sector. This included promoting the use of standardized public fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) for children and adolescents under 15 years of age. The project also trained healthcare providers and conducted continuing medical education workshops in collaboration with the Indian Academy of Pediatrics and the National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme. 7. CaP-TB field staff facilitated the notification of pediatric TB cases from private facilities and ensured the availability of medicines at local public health facilities within 1–2 days. In rural and some urban areas, frontline health workers or local NGOs delivered TB medicines directly to patients' homes. 8. Between August 2018 and June 2021, the CaP-TB project linked over 1,100 children and adolescents under 15 years of age with TB to public FDCs. The proportion of children treated with government FDCs at CaP-TB-supported sites increased from 29% to 65%. 9. Providers who switched to prescribing public FDCs cited their availability in weight-based formulations and the reduced financial burden on patients as key benefits. Regular government supply and support from the CaP-TB project also contributed to this shift. 10. Challenges included delays in treatment initiation when medicines had to be transported from district-level facilities or when senior treatment supervisors were unavailable to verify registrations. Public pharmacy hours were sometimes inconvenient for caregivers, and the pill burden for children in higher weight bands was considered excessive by some caregivers. 11. Some providers continued prescribing private-sector FDCs due to past favorable outcomes or concerns about the quality and efficacy of public-sector FDCs. Referring patients to public services also made follow-up difficult, as patients did not need to return to private facilities for medicine refills. 12. Patient preferences for private-sector medicines and privacy concerns were additional reasons for seeking care in the private sector and for providers prescribing private-sector medicines. 13. Differentiated service delivery (DSD) models, originally developed for HIV care, are people-centered approaches that simplify and adapt services to meet the diverse needs of individuals. These models can be applied to TB care, particularly for chronic diseases like TB, to enhance patient-centered care. 14. DSD models for HIV treatment include group models managed by healthcare workers or clients, as well as individual models based at facilities or in the community. These principles can be adapted to integrate TB care into DSD models. 15. Integrating TB care into DSD models requires adjustments at multiple levels of the health system, including leadership, guideline adaptation, capacity-building, logistics management, and community engagement. Local disease burden, infrastructure, and human resources must also be considered. 16. The WHO recommends delivering integrated TB and HIV services at the same time and location to improve access to high-quality care. Advances in HIV care necessitate close collaboration between NTPs and HIV programs to ensure TB services are included in DSD models. 17. Family-centered models for antiretroviral therapy (ART) that include children and caregivers can incorporate TB preventive therapy (TPT) and improve clinical outcomes for the entire family while reducing travel and costs. 18. Adherence support mechanisms, including digital technologies, can enhance TB treatment completion. However, adjustments in dispensing TB or TPT medicines are needed to align with multi-month ART dispensing. 19. Data capture and reporting mechanisms for TB care processes and outcomes are critical, especially in models not managed by health workers or based at health facilities. 20. A stable 1-year-old child living with HIV and on ART may have clinic visits every two months. TPT can be initiated during these visits, combined with TB diagnostic evaluations and education on TPT. Medicines are dispensed for two months at a time, with follow-up assessments at each visit to monitor adherence, weight changes, and potential side effects. 21. A stable 15-year-old adolescent living with HIV and on ART may have clinic visits every six months. TPT can be initiated during these visits, with a six-month supply of medicines provided. Follow-up assessments ensure adherence and completion of TPT. 22. Monthly adherence support and TB screening can be provided virtually, in the community, or through a combination of these methods to maintain the DSD model and reduce contact with health facilities.
